title: Copy-on-write and mapping files into memory
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why fork does not copy memory, demonstrate copy-on-write by counting faults, and choose correctly between MAP_SHARED and MAP_PRIVATE.

blocks.text: Two features fall out of the paging machinery, and both look impossible until you know how they work: a fork that copies gigabytes instantly, and a file you can read by dereferencing a pointer. This capstone is where the module's pieces combine.
fork does not copy your memory

The fork lesson said a child gets a copy of the parent's memory. That is what it observes, not what happens. The kernel copies only the page table, marks every writable page read-only in both processes, and returns. Nothing is duplicated. The first time either process writes to a page, the hardware traps, the kernel makes a private copy of just that page, marks it writable for the writer, and the instruction resumes.

blocks.caption: Measured: 64 MB, copied one page at a time, only when written
lines: child  RSS after fork  : 66,072 kB          <- nothing copied yet
child  RSS after writing every page : 66,644 kB   (minor faults +16,384)
parent RSS after child : 66,752 kB          <- the parent's data is untouched
# 16,384 faults x 4 KB = 64 MB. One fault per page, and only for pages written.

blocks.title: Why fork-then-exec is not wasteful
blocks.text: The pattern from the process module looks alarming — duplicate the whole process, then immediately discard it by exec'ing something else. Copy-on-write is why it costs almost nothing: between the fork and the exec, the child writes to almost no pages, so almost nothing is ever copied. The design that seemed wasteful is cheap precisely because of this mechanism.

It also explains a memory pattern that surprises people: a parent with a large heap forks a child, the child writes across that heap, and the machine's memory use climbs afterwards rather than at the moment of forking. Nothing leaked. The copies were deferred, and then they happened.
Mapping a file into your address space

mmap places a file's contents at an address range. Reading that memory reads the file — through the same demand paging as everything else, so nothing is loaded until touched. Writing it can write the file back, depending on one flag.

blocks.title: Two ways mmap fails badly
blocks.text: First: if another process truncates the file while you have it mapped, touching the removed region raises SIGBUS — a crash, not an error return, which is why network filesystems and shared temporary files are risky targets. Second: the writes you make through a MAP_SHARED mapping reach the file when the kernel decides, not when you return; msync forces them. Code that maps a file, writes, and exits without msync can lose the write if the machine goes down.

blocks.title: Prove both mechanisms
steps: Allocate 64 MB with malloc, fill it, and print RSS from /proc/self/status
fork, and in the child print RSS immediately — it should be similar, not doubled
In the child, record minor faults, write one byte per page across the whole region, and record them again
Confirm the increase is about 16,384 — the region size divided by the page size
Confirm the parent's data still holds its original values
Now create a file, map it MAP_SHARED, write through the mapping, msync, and read the file with cat
Repeat with MAP_PRIVATE and confirm the file is unchanged while the mapping shows your write
Finally map with MAP_SHARED|MAP_ANONYMOUS, fork, have the child write, and confirm the parent sees it
blocks.expected: A fork that copies nothing, a fault count that matches the region size exactly, and four clear demonstrations of what each flag means. The last one is worth remembering as a technique: MAP_SHARED|MAP_ANONYMOUS across a fork is the simplest shared memory between related processes there is.

cheatsheet: fork copies the page table, not the pages; both sides are marked read-only
The first write to a page traps and copies just that page — copy-on-write
Measured: writing 64 MB after a fork cost 16,384 faults, one per 4 KB page
fork-then-exec is cheap because the child writes almost nothing before exec
Memory use climbing after a fork, not during it, is deferred copying — not a leak
mmap maps a file into your address space; pages load on demand
MAP_SHARED: writes reach the file and other mappers. MAP_PRIVATE: writes stay yours
Verified: a MAP_PRIVATE write left the file's byte unchanged
Truncating a mapped file causes SIGBUS in the mapper — a crash, not an error code
msync forces MAP_SHARED writes out; without it, timing is the kernel's choice

checkpoint.prompt: A parent with a 4 GB heap forks. How many of its user-data pages are copied at that moment?

choices.A: It depends on how much RAM is free
choices.B: Half, on average, rounded to pages
choices.C: No user-data pages; page tables and process metadata are still copied or created

checkpoint.explanation: Only the page tables are copied and the pages are marked read-only; copying is deferred until a write. Verified: a child's resident memory right after forking a 64 MB region was unchanged, and copies happened one page at a time as it wrote.

checkpoint.prompt: You map a file MAP_PRIVATE and write through the mapping. What happens to the file?

choices.A: It is updated immediately on the write
choices.B: The write fails with an EACCES error
choices.C: It is unchanged — the write was private
choices.D: It is updated when you call munmap later

checkpoint.explanation: Your write went to a private copy of that page. Verified directly: after a MAP_PRIVATE write the mapping showed the new byte while the file still held the old one. MAP_SHARED is the flag that writes through.

checkpoint.prompt: Memory use on a server climbs sharply a few seconds after each fork, not at the fork itself. What is happening?

choices.A: Deferred copies as the child writes
choices.B: A memory leak in the child process
choices.C: The parent heap is growing on its own
choices.D: Swap is being reclaimed by the kernel

checkpoint.explanation: The fork was free precisely because the copying had not happened yet. It happens later, as the child writes to the inherited pages — which is also why the growth tracks writes rather than the fork.

checkpoint.prompt: Your process has a file mapped and another process truncates that file. What happens when you touch the removed region?

choices.A: munmap is called for you by the kernel
choices.B: You read zeros from the removed region
choices.D: The mapping shrinks automatically for you

checkpoint.explanation: There is no return value to check on a memory access, so the failure arrives as a signal. This is the main reason to be careful mapping files that others can modify.
